title: Candida Identification: Germ Tube, CHROMagar Colors and Built-In Resistance
summary: Learn how to read a true germ tube versus a pseudohypha, what the classic CHROMagar Candida colors mean and why they are only presumptive, and which yeasts and molds carry expected resistance to fluconazole or amphotericin B.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 60 Hits 5 (germ tube test), 6 (CHROMagar colors) and 7 (intrinsic antifungal resistance) and Trap 1 (germ tube vs pseudohyphae). Checked against Matare 2017, Marinho 2010, Ahmad 2012, Hospenthal 2006, Yücesoy 2003, Mendoza-Reyes 2022, Douglass 2018 and Vahedi-Shahandashti 2022 (all full text via Europe PMC). Hit 6 lists green as C. albicans; Hospenthal 2006 and Ahmad 2012 show C. dubliniensis is also green, so the lesson teaches colors as presumptive (register flag rv-ch60-chromagar-green-dubliniensis). Hit 7 calls C. lusitaniae intrinsically amphotericin B–resistant; Mendoza-Reyes 2022 describes resistance in some isolates and resistance that develops, with the species otherwise considered susceptible (register flag rv-ch60-lusitaniae-amb-not-intrinsic). The reviewer’s germ tube incubation at 35°C is not taught: the sources read used 37°C. A. terreus overlaps Trap 6, taught in micro-invasive-mold-markers. Not taught: treatment choices, MALDI-TOF identification, CHROMagar Candida Plus and C. auris.

objectives: Distinguish a true germ tube from a pseudohypha by wall geometry at the mother-cell junction.
State the classic CHROMagar Candida colors and explain why they give only a presumptive identification.
Name the expected resistance of C. krusei, C. lusitaniae and Aspergillus terreus.

scenes.title: Three yeasts, three decisions
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three yeast isolates on the bench. (1) A yeast in serum shows filaments that pinch in where they leave the mother cell. (2) A blood-culture yeast grows rough, fuzzy pink colonies on CHROMagar Candida. (3) A yeast identified as Candida lusitaniae comes from a patient already on amphotericin B. Question token: “Germ tube? Which species? Which drug trap?”

cues.text: Three yeasts reach the bench. The first, in serum, sprouts filaments that pinch in where they leave the mother cell.
The second grows rough, fuzzy pink colonies on CHROMagar Candida. The third is Candida lusitaniae, from a patient already on amphotericin B.
Is the first a germ tube? What is the second? And what drug trap hides in the third?

props.label: Germ tube? Which species? Which drug trap?

scenes.title: The germ tube test
scenes.altText: Schematic: two yeast cells in serum. Method card: a few colonies in a small volume of serum (human, fetal bovine or other animal serum in the studies read), incubated at 37°C and examined at about 2.5–3 hours. Left drawing: a true germ tube — a slender outgrowth with straight, parallel walls and NO constriction where it leaves the mother cell. Right drawing: a pseudohypha — a bud that stays attached, with a constricted neck at the junction. Result card: a positive germ tube presumptively identifies Candida albicans or Candida dubliniensis, which share this trait.

cues.text: The germ tube test is quick: a few colonies go into a small volume of serum at thirty-seven degrees, and a drop is examined at about two and a half to three hours.
A true germ tube is a slender outgrowth with straight, parallel walls, and no constriction where it leaves the mother cell.
A pseudohypha looks similar at a glance, but it is an elongated bud with a constricted neck at the junction. That pinch means pseudohypha, not germ tube.
A positive germ tube is a presumptive identification: Candida albicans or Candida dubliniensis, which both form germ tubes in serum.

props.title: Pseudohypha
lines: Constricted neck = not a germ tube

scenes.title: Reading CHROMagar Candida
scenes.altText: Schematic CHROMagar Candida plate. Chromogenic substrates in the medium react with enzymes made by the yeast, so colonies develop colors. Manufacturer claims, as reported by Hospenthal 2006: after 48 hours at 30–37°C, C. albicans = green; C. tropicalis = steel blue; C. krusei = fuzzy, rose-pink (rough, spreading) colonies. Caveats card: C. dubliniensis also grows green; most other species tested in that study gave pink, lavender or ivory colonies; some species (C. inconspicua, some C. firmetaria) mimic C. krusei. Colors are presumptive and confirmation needs further identification methods.

cues.text: CHROMagar Candida contains chromogenic substrates. Enzymes made by each yeast split them, so colonies grow in different colors, read after about forty-eight hours.
The three classic colors: green for Candida albicans, steel blue for Candida tropicalis, and rough, fuzzy, rose-pink spreading colonies for Candida krusei.
But green is not proof of albicans: Candida dubliniensis grows green too. In one study most other species tested gave pink, lavender or ivory colonies, and a few mimicked the rough pink of krusei.
So a CHROMagar color is a presumptive identification. It speeds the answer, but confirmation needs another identification method.

scenes.title: Resistance you should expect
scenes.altText: Three resistance cards. C. krusei (the same species as Pichia kudriavzevii): innate resistance to fluconazole in most isolates. C. lusitaniae: some isolates are resistant to amphotericin B and the species can develop resistance during therapy; it is generally considered susceptible to azoles and flucytosine. Aspergillus terreus: most isolates have high amphotericin B MICs and are considered intrinsically resistant (some isolates have low MICs); infection is often refractory to amphotericin B and has a high propensity to disseminate. Hook answers: (1) constriction = pseudohypha, not a germ tube; (2) rough fuzzy pink = presumptive C. krusei, avoid relying on fluconazole; (3) C. lusitaniae on amphotericin B: watch for emerging resistance.

cues.text: Some species carry resistance you should expect. Candida krusei, the same species as Pichia kudriavzevii, has innate resistance to fluconazole.
Candida lusitaniae is different: some isolates resist amphotericin B, and resistance can emerge during therapy. The species is generally considered susceptible to azoles and flucytosine.
Among molds, Aspergillus terreus usually shows high amphotericin B MICs, is considered intrinsically resistant, and tends to disseminate.

Back to the hook. The pinched filaments are pseudohyphae. The fuzzy pink isolate is presumptive krusei, so fluconazole is a poor choice. And the lusitaniae patient on amphotericin B needs a watch for emerging resistance.

lines: 2 Fuzzy pink = presumptive krusei: not fluconazole
3 Lusitaniae on amphotericin B: watch resistance

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Any filament from a yeast in serum = positive germ tube” (✓ only parallel walls with no constriction; a pinched junction is a pseudohypha); “Green on CHROMagar = C. albicans” (✓ C. dubliniensis is also green; colors are presumptive); “C. lusitaniae is always amphotericin B–resistant” (✓ some isolates are resistant and resistance can emerge; test, don’t assume either way).

cues.text: Trap one: any filament from a yeast in serum is a positive germ tube. No: only parallel walls with no constriction count. A pinch at the junction is a pseudohypha.
Trap two: a green colony on CHROMagar is Candida albicans. No: Candida dubliniensis is green too, and every color is presumptive.
Trap three: Candida lusitaniae is always resistant to amphotericin B. No: some isolates are, and resistance can emerge on therapy, so test rather than assume.

props.title: ✗ “Green = C. albicans.”
lines: ✓ C. dubliniensis is green too: presumptive

props.title: ✗ “C. lusitaniae always resists amphotericin B.”

scenes.title: Straw, not sausage links
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “A true germ tube is a STRAW, not a string of SAUSAGE LINKS: straight sides, no pinch. Green has a TWIN (albicans and dubliniensis). Krusei KEEPS OUT fluconazole; Lusitaniae can LEARN to resist amphotericin B; Terreus is TOUGH against amphotericin B.” Tokens: straw = germ tube · green twins · krusei keeps out fluconazole. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: a true germ tube is a straw, not a string of sausage links. Green has a twin, albicans and dubliniensis. Krusei keeps out fluconazole, lusitaniae can learn to resist amphotericin B, and terreus is tough against it.
Where it breaks: colors and germ tubes are only presumptive and need confirmation; other species can mimic krusei; and lusitaniae resistance is not universal, so susceptibility testing decides.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Color and germ tube are presumptive

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Germ tube: parallel walls, no pinch → albicans or dubliniensis”, “Colors presumptive · krusei: fluconazole · lusitaniae, terreus: amphotericin B”.

cues.text: Call a germ tube only when the filament has parallel walls and no constriction, treat CHROMagar colors as presumptive because Candida dubliniensis grows green too, and expect Candida krusei to resist fluconazole while Candida lusitaniae and Aspergillus terreus can defeat amphotericin B.

props.label: Germ tube: parallel walls, no pinch → albicans or dubliniensis
Colors presumptive · krusei: fluconazole · lusitaniae, terreus: AmB

explanation.what: Plain language: when a yeast grows, labs use quick tricks to guess the species. In serum, Candida albicans sprouts a straight tube; on a special colored agar, different species grow in different colors. Some species are known to shrug off certain antifungal drugs, so naming the species early helps. Scientific terms: germ tube, pseudohypha, presumptive identification, Candida dubliniensis, chromogenic medium (CHROMagar Candida), chromogenic substrate, intrinsic (innate) resistance, acquired resistance, minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), Pichia kudriavzevii.
explanation.why: Germ tubes form as a true outgrowth with no septum or constriction at the origin, while pseudohyphae are elongated buds that stay attached at a constricted neck. Chromogenic substrates are split by species-associated enzymes, but enzyme patterns overlap, so colors only suggest a species. C. krusei carries innate fluconazole resistance; C. lusitaniae can switch or evolve to amphotericin B resistance; most A. terreus isolates have high amphotericin B MICs.
explanation.measure: Germ tube: colonies in serum at 37°C, examined at about 2.5–3 h in the studies read; positive = slender tube, parallel walls, no constriction → presumptive C. albicans or C. dubliniensis. CHROMagar Candida (manufacturer claims as reported, 48 h at 30–37°C): green = C. albicans, steel blue = C. tropicalis, rough fuzzy rose-pink = C. krusei; C. dubliniensis also green; other species pink, lavender or ivory.
explanation.differs: Germ tube (parallel walls, no constriction) vs pseudohypha (constricted neck); C. albicans vs C. dubliniensis (both germ tube positive and green); innate resistance (C. krusei to fluconazole; A. terreus to amphotericin B) vs resistance in some isolates or emerging on therapy (C. lusitaniae to amphotericin B).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: interpret a germ tube with or without constriction, name the species for a CHROMagar color, or pick the drug a species is expected to resist.

comparisons.title: Germ tube vs pseudohypha
comparisons.distinguisher: Wall geometry at the mother-cell junction, not whether something protrudes.

comparisons.title: Expected resistance

left.label: Innate
points: A. terreus: amphotericin B (most isolates high MICs)

comparisons.distinguisher: Whether resistance is expected in most isolates of the species, or only in some isolates and those that adapt on treatment.

mnemonic.text: A true germ tube is a STRAW, not a string of SAUSAGE LINKS. Green has a TWIN (albicans and dubliniensis). Krusei KEEPS OUT fluconazole; Lusitaniae can LEARN to resist amphotericin B; Terreus is TOUGH against amphotericin B.
mnemonic.explanation: Links the germ tube geometry, the shared green color and the three resistance patterns.
mnemonic.limitation: A germ tube is not a hollow straw and pseudohyphae are not literal sausages; the image only marks straight sides versus a pinch. Colors and germ tubes are presumptive and need confirmation; other species can mimic C. krusei; C. lusitaniae resistance is not universal, so susceptibility testing decides.

analogyLimitations: Yeast drawings and the plate are schematic; real colony shades vary by isolate, time and temperature.
CHROMagar colors are manufacturer claims as reported in one study.
takeaway: Call a germ tube only when the filament has parallel walls and no constriction, treat CHROMagar colors as presumptive because Candida dubliniensis grows green too, and expect Candida krusei to resist fluconazole while Candida lusitaniae and Aspergillus terreus can defeat amphotericin B.

questions.stem: After incubation in serum at 37°C, a yeast shows elongated outgrowths that are clearly constricted where they join the mother cell. How should this be read?

options.text: Not a true germ tube; these are pseudohyphae
options.rationale: Correct. A constricted neck at the junction marks a pseudohypha; a germ tube has parallel walls and no constriction.

options.text: Positive germ tube; report C. albicans
options.rationale: Incorrect. Any outgrowth is not enough; the constriction rules out a true germ tube.

options.text: Positive germ tube; report C. dubliniensis
options.rationale: Incorrect. C. dubliniensis does form germ tubes, but these constricted forms are not germ tubes.

options.text: Positive germ tube; report C. krusei
options.rationale: Incorrect. The germ tube is a presumptive marker of C. albicans or C. dubliniensis, and this result is not a germ tube anyway.

questions.stem: A germ tube–positive yeast grows green colonies on CHROMagar Candida. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Presumptive C. albicans or C. dubliniensis; confirm with another method if species matters
options.rationale: Correct. Both species form germ tubes and grow green, so both tests are presumptive.
Incorrect. C. dubliniensis shares both the germ tube and the green color.
Incorrect. C. tropicalis is described as steel blue on this medium.
Incorrect. C. krusei grows rough, fuzzy, rose-pink colonies.

options.text: C. krusei: innate resistance to fluconazole
options.rationale: Correct. C. krusei (Pichia kudriavzevii) is described as innately fluconazole resistant.

options.text: C. lusitaniae: every isolate intrinsically resistant to fluconazole
options.rationale: Incorrect. C. lusitaniae is generally considered azole susceptible; its known problem is amphotericin B resistance in some isolates.

options.text: Aspergillus terreus: reliably killed by amphotericin B
options.rationale: Incorrect. Most A. terreus isolates have high amphotericin B MICs and infection is often refractory to it.

options.text: C. albicans: innate resistance to fluconazole
options.rationale: Incorrect. The sources read describe innate fluconazole resistance in C. krusei, not in C. albicans.

accuracyFlags.issue: Hit 6 gives green on CHROMagar as C. albicans; Hospenthal 2006 and Ahmad 2012 show C. dubliniensis also grows green, so the color is presumptive for either species. The lesson teaches both.

Hit 7 lists C. lusitaniae as intrinsically amphotericin B–resistant; Mendoza-Reyes 2022 describes resistance in some isolates and resistance that develops, with the species otherwise considered susceptible. The lesson teaches “some isolates; can emerge on therapy”.
